Computational Concepts in HCDE: Python Tools for Design Research

HCDE 530 Computational Concepts in HCDE, University of Washington, Spring 2026. Individual work.

HCDE 530 introduced the computational concepts and AI-assisted programming skills that design research increasingly depends on: cleaning messy data, pulling data from web APIs, analyzing it with pandas, visualizing it, and critically evaluating what AI tools produce. I worked in Cursor with Python and Jupyter notebooks, alongside Claude as a coding partner, and documented every week’s work in a public GitHub repository, mapping each piece to the course’s competencies.

Survey theme report: a first pass at open-ended responses

After a survey closes, a UX researcher can spend hours reading and hand-grouping open-ended answers before synthesis even begins. For my final mini project, I built a Python tool that automates that first pass. It reads any survey CSV, finds the columns that hold long written answers (or uses the ones you name), groups similar answers into themes, and writes a ranked report with each theme’s frequency, keywords, and representative quotes, ready to sort in a spreadsheet or bring into a workshop.

  1. Survey CSVAny export with open-ended questions
  2. Find text columnsAuto-detected, or named with a flag
  3. Group into themesTF–IDF and K-means clustering
  4. Ranked reportThemes, frequency, keywords, quotes
Top themes from a run on the public Food Choices survey sample (125 responses)
Survey questionTheme keywordsShare of answersExample answer
Ideal diethealthy, diet, eat, fruits87%“My ideal diet would be a healthy diet. I would eat meats and veggies.”
Eating changeseat, food, meals, healthy77%“They have gotten very bad. I eat a lot more food that I know I should not eat.”
Childhood foodpizza, chicken, spaghetti, steak55%“Pizza”
Comfort food reasonsboredom, happiness, sadness, hunger41%“Boredom, happiness, distraught”

I made a few deliberate scoping decisions. The tool is file-first, because CSV exports are what teams already pass around, and it keeps API keys out of the main workflow. I chose TF–IDF and K-means over heavier models because they run offline, behave predictably on small samples, and are explainable to stakeholders. I tested on a public dataset with the same shape as a real survey export, mixing numeric and text columns, so I wouldn’t need to share sensitive participant responses. And because real exports are messy, the loader tries several text encodings and line endings, treats placeholders like “nan” and “none” as missing, and screens out Likert-style numeric columns. A fixed random seed means the same file always produces the same report.

Just as important is what the tool doesn’t claim. Its themes are statistical clusters, not a research codebook, and keyword labels can flatten sarcasm, cultural context, or multilingual answers. I built in ways for researchers to override it, such as naming the exact columns to analyze or setting the number of themes, and I’d describe its output to a stakeholder as a fast exploratory pass: prioritized reading, not a decision engine. Anyone can run it in the browser through Google Colab without installing anything. Next, I would add a simple upload-and-download web page for non-developers, plus controls for cluster quality and non-English text.

Run it in Google ColabRead the code and documentation

Open Brewery DB: what the data can and can’t say

For my first mini project, I pulled about 5,000 records from the Open Brewery DB API, cleaned them down to 4,310 U.S. breweries, and asked three questions: how brewery types are distributed across states, whether micro, regional, and brewpub breweries concentrate in particular regions, and whether cities with more breweries have a more diverse mix of types. I chose each chart to match the shape of its question and wrote a title that states the finding.

The clearest pattern: cities with more listed breweries tend to list more distinct types, yet many large cities still draw 50–70% of their listings from a single type, so a bigger scene doesn’t mean an even mix. Micro breweries and brewpubs dominate nationally, the West has the most listings of all three focus types, and the Northeast has the fewest. For every chart, I wrote down what a reader could misread and what a flat or null result would still tell us. Open Brewery DB is a community-maintained listing, not a census, so raw counts reflect how thoroughly a place is listed as much as its actual market, and association at the city level says nothing about cause.

Read the analysis notebook

Along the way

Weekly exercises built toward these projects: documenting a script so that both people and AI tools could follow its intent, pulling my first data from an API (and diagnosing an HTTP 403 error by adding request headers), and debugging a messy survey file with two bugs. One crashed on the word “fifteen” in a years-of-experience column. The other ran without complaint while printing the lowest scores under a “Top 5” label. That second bug taught me that code that runs isn’t necessarily code that’s right, and that checking output against the question is part of the work.

Forterra: A Visual System for Pacific Northwest Land Stewardship

HCDE 508 Visual Communication, University of Washington, Spring 2026. Client redesign for Forterra, a Washington land conservation nonprofit.

For HCDE 508, I spent the quarter designing a complete visual system for Forterra, a Washington nonprofit that has stewarded land in the Pacific Northwest for more than three decades. My goal was a system that feels like it has been there just as long. Every major decision came back to one question: is this actually serving the work Forterra does?

I started with secondary research on Forterra’s mission, audiences, channels, and competitors. Forterra is unusual in combining land conservation, housing, climate, and equity work, which sets it apart from organizations like The Nature Conservancy and Trust for Public Land but makes its mission hard to communicate simply. Its existing site was clean, organized, and nature-forward, but its messaging was dense, its hierarchy weak, and its personality muted. That gave me three goals: clarify the core message, humanize the brand, and lean on visual storytelling. From there, I built the system one layer at a time, from layout, type, and color to imagery and the logo, then brought it together in a style guide and applied it across three surfaces.

Layout and type: built for reading, not scanning

I designed an editorial, slow-paced layout as a deliberate counter to the urgency I see by default in most nonprofit websites. It rests on a 12-column grid with generous 80–120px gaps between sections, a stable three-column module for cards and stats, and predictable zones that move from narrative to supporting content to action. The pacing asks Forterra’s primary audiences, donors and policy stakeholders, to read rather than skim. The type pairing carries the message that we have been here a long time and we know what we are doing: Times headings for institutional permanence, like a land trust’s annual report, and Helvetica body text for honesty and directness. Hierarchy comes from moderate differences in size and spacing rather than heavy weights, and italics are left out of the system entirely.

Where we work

Diverse landscapes, connected communities.

From the Cascade foothills to the Yakima basin, from urban creek corridors to coastal estuaries, Forterra works across Washington’s most vital landscapes.

Donate

Times headings, Helvetica body, Moss Green eyebrow above a Warm Stone rule, Harvest Orange reserved for action

Color: restraint as strategy

The palette argues that restraint is strategy. Parchment is the dominant surface because it introduces warmth before a single word is read, keeping the system from feeling clinical or corporate. Forest Midnight has just enough green in it to connect to nature without announcing itself. Harvest Orange appears in only two or three places on a page, reserved for calls to action like Donate. If everything is important, nothing is, and its scarcity is what gives it urgency. Choosing this palette was the hardest decision of the project. My other direction, Living Green, was more expressive and immediately appealing, but Rooted and Warm was the right fit for Forterra and its audience, and choosing it meant designing for them rather than for the feeling I personally found appealing. The system is simple enough to memorize: dark text goes on Parchment, green marks structure, orange marks action, and stone marks metadata.

  • ParchmentRGB 245, 240, 228The dominant surface: page canvas, sections, and cards
  • Forest MidnightRGB 28, 38, 28All text and the navigation bar
  • Moss GreenRGB 88, 112, 72Structure: section eyebrows, accents, active states
  • Warm StoneRGB 168, 158, 132Quiet details: dividers, captions, metadata
  • Harvest OrangeRGB 212, 88, 30Action only, like the Donate button

Target proportions across a page: Parchment 55%, Forest Midnight 30%, Moss Green 10%, Warm Stone 4%, Harvest Orange 1%

Imagery: Witnessed Land

I wanted every photograph to feel as if it were made by someone who belongs to the place, not by a visiting documentarian. I called this direction Witnessed Land. Defining it made it easy to rule images out, so I wrote exclusion rules alongside inclusion rules. Most systems only define the latter, and taking an opinionated position about what Forterra is not felt like a risk, but it is what gives the system character and sets it apart from other environmental nonprofits. Photos receive a consistent, restrained treatment: highlights pulled back, shadows lifted, saturation reduced 10–15%, and a faint warm cast in the midtones to echo Parchment and Warm Stone.

Included
  • People doing something, with the land present
  • Volunteers who aren’t looking at the camera
  • Eye-level photos with room to breathe
  • Muted greens and overcast skies
  • Archival images that carry institutional memory
Excluded
  • Saturated drone shots that aestheticize the land
  • Golden-hour hero shots and peak foliage
  • Distant vantage points that lose presence
  • Posed group photos that read as stock
  • Pristine wilderness as aspiration

Logo: one living form

After sketching and digitizing several directions, I chose a mark in which the capital F is also a tree, with roots, trunk, and branches drawn as one continuous organic form. It won because the letterform and the nature symbol read as a single idea rather than two layered ones, which also makes it more durable. Critique pushed me to refine it: I brought it closer to the natural, modern feel of my moodboard, removed the doubled F in the wordmark for readability, flattened the tree’s extra hues, and cut an ornamental divider that wasn’t serving the direction.

The system in context

I applied the system to a homepage, an email newsletter, and a new Where We Work page, then documented it in a style guide styled to match the brand. The Where We Work page shows the system’s flexibility: it trades the homepage’s column grid for full-bleed landscape bands, yet uses the exact same type scale, color rules, eyebrow pattern, and image overlay treatment, so it’s still recognizably Forterra.

Iteration shaped every surface. My original homepage hero image was too busy and failed contrast, and the replacement fixed readability while strengthening the Witnessed Land direction. I also tightened spacing, removed duplicated copy, and fixed CTA buttons that didn’t meet accessibility standards.

The style guide closes with accessibility annotations for each surface: heading structure, landmark regions, alt text, reading and tab order, form labels, and touch targets. Annotating the homepage meant mapping all 27 keyboard stops in visual order, starting with a skip link, and flagging every button that fell short of the 44-pixel minimum touch target so it could be fixed in production. Technically, it was the hardest part of the project.

“It’s very easy to add to the page, but much harder to remove, simplify, or trust the negative space you’re seeing.”

From my final presentation

I started this course thinking of visual identity as mostly an aesthetic exercise. By the end, I was making decisions about contrast ratios, landmark regions, and orphaned text, and annotating accessibility taught me that a visual system has to communicate function, not just feeling. I also learned to push back on my own instincts productively, which I now see as the mark of design judgment rather than personal preference.

The Housing Crisis Is Unequal and Political: Counter-Visualizing Bay Area Housing Burden

Design Research Group on countervisualizations, University of Washington, Spring 2026. Individual project.

In Spring 2026, I joined a Design Research Group exploring how critical, feminist traditions of resistance and refusal can inform the design of countervisualizations: visualizations that push back on misleading political claims and humanize underrepresented people. Alongside reading research on countervisualizations, anthropographics, and feminist epistemologies, and contributing reflections toward a conference manuscript, I designed a pair of visualizations about Bay Area housing to put those ideas into practice.

The dominant story about Bay Area housing is deceptively simple: costs have risen because the region is desirable, the tech economy has grown, and supply hasn’t kept pace. It circulates through regional planning documents, policy briefs, and mainstream news, almost always told through aggregates like median rent and countywide burden rates. That story isn’t false, since supply constraints are real, but it’s incomplete in a way that frames rising costs as a neutral market outcome rather than a policy outcome, and it obscures who actually bears them.

Two visualizations, one dataset

I built two visualizations from the same five county-level CSVs: the Metropolitan Transportation Commission’s Vital Signs housing affordability extracts, derived from the American Community Survey. The first deliberately replicates the dominant frame. It charts the share of renter households paying at least 35% of income on housing in each county from 2009 to 2024, with clean lines, a neutral palette, minimal annotation, and no explicit argument, just as it might appear in a planning report.

The counter-visualization, titled “The housing crisis is unequal and political,” makes an unusual move: it states what the data cannot show before showing what it can. Its data scope note names the absences up front: no race or ethnicity, no neighborhood geography, no voucher coverage, and no displacement indicators. From there, it adds an income-stratified layer to a schematic county map with a timeline slider, an income ladder for each county, and callouts that link to the regional and state sources needed to go further.

Disaggregating by income reveals the sharpest signal these files contain. In 2024, households earning under $10,000 pay more than 30% of their income on housing at rates of roughly 91–100% in every Bay Area county. Among households earning $100,000 or more, it’s roughly 13–20%. That gap is the ethical center of what these spreadsheets can support, and an aggregate trend line dissolves it into a county average.

A narrower, more honest claim

I originally set out to show racial displacement, but this data can’t support that claim. So I narrowed it: aggregate renter burden statistics obscure profound inequality by income, and the people most exposed to housing cost stress are systematically the least visible in headline affordability metrics. I also stated what would falsify it: evidence that burden rates across income groups have converged. The 2024 data doesn’t support that alternative. Using exactly the data behind the dominant frame, rather than a different dataset, makes the larger point that the dominant framing is a choice, not a necessity.

A counter-visualization makes its own choices, too, so I tried to name them. I foreground the income gap rather than the fact that several counties, including San Francisco, show lower severe-burden shares in 2024 than in 2009, and the callouts explain why that improvement doesn’t disprove displacement pressure. I also named a misappropriation risk: a county shaded by high low-income burden could be read by investors as a map of acquisition targets. And I acknowledged that the implied audience is students, advocates, planners, and journalists, not the communities most burdened by housing costs. Making inequality legible to people with political power is different work from designing with displaced residents themselves.

Whose story this is

Every voice in both visualizations is institutional. Neither includes testimony from renters or displaced communities, so the story is told about people at the bottom of the income distribution, not by or with them. The data also understates what it shows: the American Community Survey undercounts undocumented immigrants, people in informal or overcrowded housing, and unhoused people, and it says nothing about displacement before 2009 or the history of redlining, urban renewal, and restrictive covenants that shaped these patterns.

I live in the Bay Area and am not a neutral observer of this data. I chose the topic because of that tension, not despite it. My commitment isn’t to a particular policy position but to the premise that aggregate affordability metrics are a political choice, and that disaggregating by income, and next by race and geography, is a moral act rather than a methodological flourish. The question “who is burdened?” is inseparable from the question of what counts as a housing crisis in the first place.

ORIS Usability Study: Award Activity by Cost Center

HCDE 517 Usability Studies, University of Washington, Winter 2026. Client: UW Office of Research Information Services. Team: Yue Xu, Ana Bungag, Riya Chaudhari, Nina Nguyen.

For HCDE 517: Usability Studies, my team partnered with the University of Washington’s Office of Research Information Services (ORIS) to evaluate the Award Activity by Cost Center report in the UW BI Portal. The report helps Principal Investigators (PIs) and research administration staff track how awarded funding changes over time and compare it across schools, departments, and labs. Early interviews had shown strong interest in a report like this, yet after launch, adoption stayed low. ORIS wanted to understand why.

We framed the study around three questions: can people find the report, can they run it, and does what it shows actually help them? Each of us first ran an independent heuristic evaluation against Nielsen’s 10 usability heuristics, and we synthesized our observations through affinity mapping in FigJam. We then mapped the report’s user flows and ran remote, moderated think-aloud sessions over Zoom with four research administration staff from the College of Engineering, the School of Medicine, and the Department of Biostatistics: two current users and two new users. Each hour-long session walked through three tasks (locate the report, filter and run it, and interpret an award’s status) paired with post-task ease and confidence ratings.

Navigation worked: all four participants found the report, through either search or the catalog. Friction began at the filters. Every participant wanted more flexibility in searching, filtering, and scrolling, and three of four were thrown by fields the system had pre-populated. Asterisks implied every field was required, and the default selections left people double-checking results they no longer trusted. Once the report ran, everyone found the table clear, but three of four said it was missing details their work depends on, especially for large awards split across departments.

HighlightIssueIdea

Task 1: Find the report

  • High success rate 4/4
  • Helpful categorization
  • Difficulty searching without exact keywords 2/3
  • Show whether data is up to date 1/3

Task 2: Filter and run it

  • Familiar filter names 3/4
  • Too little flexibility 4/4
  • Confusing pre-populated selections 3/4
  • Unpredictable collapsible panel 1/4
  • Save filter selections 1/4

Task 3: Read the results

  • Clear results table 4/4
  • Missing useful data 3/4
  • Too little modification detail 3/4
  • Unexplained blank entries 3/4
  • Misleading download icon 1/4
  • Exports that break Excel workflows 1/4

“Different departments manage different sub-budgets within same award and all have different statuses. So if managing that kind of big award, this is unfortunately not going to be helpful with the current design.”

Participant 3

We recommended making filters searchable and empty by default, with saved configurations for reports people run again and again; clearer required-field indicators, system status, and error messages; richer modification and financial detail with a “last updated” timestamp; Excel-friendly exports without merged headers; and co-design sessions with end users, including PIs.

One theme surfaced in every session: participants felt the report had been shaped by leadership rather than by the people who use it day to day. This project showed me how much a usability study depends on domain fluency. Our unfamiliarity with research administration was the biggest early hurdle, and working closely with ORIS staff is what let us ask sharper questions. Pairing heuristic evaluation with live testing also showed me how two methods can confirm and sharpen each other. With more time, I would recruit PIs, whom we couldn’t schedule within the course timeline, and reach our original goal of ten participants.

The Paradox of Support: How Caregivers of Children with Autism Perceive Social Support

HCDE 519 Qualitative Research Methods, University of Washington, Winter 2026. Team: Emily Kragel, Rebecca Mueller, Riya Chaudhari, Samantha Wobst.

For HCDE 519: Qualitative Research Methods, a studio course on choosing, applying, and triangulating qualitative methods, my team designed and ran a study with caregivers of children with autism. Social support is usually framed as something caregivers receive. Our secondary research pointed to a paradox instead: the same structures meant to help can also create new labor, dependencies, and emotional weight. We wanted to understand that tension from the caregiver’s side.

How do caregivers perceive the social support they receive in caring for their child(ren) with autism?

  • How does social support alleviate stress or provide joy to parents?
  • How does social support introduce additional work or stress?

Our questions sharpened as we went. We started out asking broadly which tools and services exist and whether they help. The literature pushed us toward perceived support, centered on how caregivers themselves make meaning of it, and toward holding both directions at once: support that sustains and support that depletes.

We worked with three caregivers whose lives spanned different countries, family structures, and children’s ages, from early childhood to young adulthood. Each took part in a photo diary, taking one photo a day for a week of something meaningful in their parenting journey, followed by a photo-elicitation interview in which they walked us through each image. Partway through each interview, we ran a card sort built live from the support resources they had named, placing each one on a Miro board by how accessible and how valuable it felt. Participation in the diary varied widely, from 13 photos to none, and some people shared photos they already had instead of new ones. We treated whatever each person brought as a starting point rather than a prerequisite, and the photos people chose to share became meaningful in their own right. To keep our interpretations grounded, we traced every finding from interview excerpts to interpretive codes to themes.

Support is often limited by conditionality or misalignment

Informal networks of friends, family, and faith communities were present and well-intentioned, but the help they offered rarely matched what families needed most. Support flowed toward socially comfortable forms of help, while hands-on care, real inclusion, and coordination of complex routines went unmet. Even a shared diagnosis didn’t guarantee shared understanding, since needs vary so widely across the spectrum.

What support systems offerWhat families often need
Emotional encouragementReliable respite care
Social connectionSkilled childcare
Offers of helpStructured coordination of routines
Occasional, or on-paper-only, inclusionConsistent and meaningful inclusion

Without reliable support, caregivers take on the work themselves

Caregivers regained a sense of control through anticipatory planning, constant learning, and coordination across schools, therapies, paperwork, and family. They pre-checked whether activities were accessible, trained relatives, searched everything from formal training programs to Instagram for strategies, and stepped into roles they had never imagined. The stability they achieved came from their own effort, not from the systems around them. Support didn’t remove the burden; it shifted it.

“I had never ice skated in my life, but in order to have a coach work with her, I had to put on my ice skates and get out there so that I could help them figure out how to communicate with her.”

Participant 1

Rare alignment inspires extraordinary gratitude

When caregivers did find someone truly attuned to their child, the gratitude was profound. Alignment emerged through highly specific shared identities, like fellow musician parents or parents of children who are also blind; through institutional champions, like a coach who created a special performance; and through professionals who became family over years of shared milestones. But it also revealed a fragility: meaningful support often depended on who a family happened to meet rather than being built into the system, and could disappear when a person moved on or a program ended.

“She was his teaching assistant, but she became like family.”

Participant 3

From these findings, we described what meaningful support looks like, as a lens for designers, service providers, and schools:

  • Has alignment
  • Is adaptable
  • Is flexible, not conditional
  • Limits coordination burden
  • Has relational continuity
  • Promotes caregiver restoration

For design practice, this means focusing on fit over quantity, moving past statements of inclusion to practical, adaptive support, and designing around the coordination burden that caregivers currently carry. For future research, we identified open questions about the boundary between formal and informal support (when a professional role becomes a relationship) and about the guilt that makes self-care feel out of reach.

I wrote our report’s introduction and contributed to our key findings write-ups. I began this project assuming that support structures would mainly be sources of relief. As the interviews unfolded, it became clear they could also introduce new responsibilities, dependencies, and emotional tensions, and noticing my own assumptions shift was as valuable as the research process itself. It changed how I think about support: less as service infrastructure and more as a relational, negotiated experience shaped by alignment, trust, and connection. Our sample of three was small and professionally similar, so these findings can’t speak for all caregivers, but they gave us rich, detailed insight into lives that are too often simplified.

Rainiest Kingdom Detective

MS Human Centered Design and Engineering, University of Washington

As part of my coursework for my Masters of Science in Human Centered Design and Engineering at the University of Washington, Rainiest Kingdom Detective is a narrative-driven mobile game designed to teach children and parents about online data privacy through interactive, repeatable gameplay. The experience transforms abstract privacy concepts into concrete decisions using storytelling, adaptive difficulty, and co-play mechanics. Built through user interviews, focus groups, and usability testing, the project emphasizes intentional education, emotional awareness, and transparency in digital literacy for families.

Research revealed a disconnect between high concern and low confidence among parents regarding children’s online safety, and a lack of practical, engaging education for children. Existing solutions relied heavily on passive information or monitoring tools that failed to build understanding or agency. Using these insights, my team developed the following design question to guide us: “How might we support parents and children (ages 10–18) in protecting children online through an educational approach that maintains control and agency over their digital footprints?”

The final prototype demonstrates how education-first design can replace fear-based or control-heavy approaches to online safety. Usability testing showed increased engagement, stronger understanding of privacy concepts, and positive feedback around the narrative and reward systems. This project strengthened my ability to translate complex policy and technical concepts into approachable experiences, design systems that balance education, motivation, and emotional context, as well as collaborate across research, interaction design, and storytelling. If expanded further, I would explore additional advanced privacy topics, deepen adaptive learning logic, and validate long-term behavior change through longitudinal testing.

Receipt Recipes

AI-powered meal planning concept

Receipt Recipes is an AI-powered meal planning concept that transforms grocery receipts into personalized recipe recommendations. By automatically scanning and parsing receipts, the product eliminates manual ingredient entry and helps users reduce food waste, save time, and plan meals more effectively. Designed through market research, user surveys, and strategic product planning, Receipt Recipes demonstrates an end-to-end product vision, from problem discovery to MVP definition and roadmap execution.

Meal planning often breaks down after grocery shopping. People forget what they bought, struggle to come up with meal ideas, or let ingredients expire, leading to wasted food, time, and money. Receipt Recipes explores how grocery data can be transformed into actionable, personalized meal planning through automation and AI. The product concept is a mobile app that scans grocery receipts, automatically identifies purchased ingredients, and generates tailored recipes based on dietary needs, preferences, and real purchasing behavior.

Despite widespread use of digital recipes and meal-planning tools, most solutions rely on manual ingredient entry or generic meal plans that don’t reflect what users actually buy. This disconnect contributes to food waste and decision fatigue, especially for busy professionals, students, and households with dietary restrictions. The proposed MVP allows users to:

  • Upload or scan grocery receipts
  • Automatically extract ingredients using OCR
  • Match ingredients to a structured database
  • Receive curated recipes based on dietary needs and preferences
  • Save receipt and recipe history for future reference

The long-term vision expands into pantry tracking, expiration reminders, and sustainability insights.

The final concept demonstrates how automation and personalization can reduce cognitive load in everyday decision-making. Research validated both user interest and willingness to pay, while strategic planning translated a broad idea into a buildable, scalable product. This project strengthened my ability to translate a personal pain point into a validated market opportunity, balance ambition with feasibility through MVP scoping, communicate complex systems clearly across documentation, and think holistically about user needs, business goals, and technical constraints. Given more time, I would conduct usability testing on early prototypes and validate long-term behavioral impact on food waste reduction.

Imagined Futures: Cultural Narratives Shaping AI Development

UC Davis Center for Artificial Intelligence and Experimental Futures (CAIEF)

I collaborated with the UC Davis Center for Artificial Intelligence and Experimental Futures (CAIEF) to build a structured research corpus analyzing how cultural narratives and imagined futures influence AI development. This project examined how science fiction, media discourse, policy documents, and public imagination shape real-world AI design decisions. I supported corpus construction, data organization, and exploratory analysis using RStudio and Git-based workflows.

AI systems reflect the narratives and imagined futures embedded in culture. Understanding these narratives helps us critically examine bias, power, and long-term societal impact in AI systems. This project strengthened my ability to critically interrogate the assumptions embedded in technology development and design for more inclusive, equitable futures.

UC Davis Design Interactive Fellowship: MyUCDavis Redesign

UC Davis Design Interactive Fellowship

My team undertook a comprehensive redesign of our university’s online student portal with the goals of improving usability and accessibility. The project involved extensive user research, where we conducted surveys and usability tests to better understand student needs. We then developed wireframes, interactive prototypes, and high-fidelity mockups that prioritized clarity, ease of navigation, and mobile responsiveness. Throughout the project, I played a key role in synthesizing research insights, refining information architecture, and designing key interface components. I helped translate user needs into actionable design solutions, ensuring that our prototypes told the stories of its users. Through this experience, I strengthened my skills in user research, prototyping, usability testing, and cross-functional collaboration, while also gaining firsthand experience in designing for a large-scale digital platform.

ECS170: Artificial Intelligence Final Project — Breast Cancer Classification Model

UC Davis

This project focused on developing a machine learning model to predict breast cancer diagnoses based on patient diagnostic characteristics. Using a dataset from Kaggle, my team and I analyzed ten key tumor features to classify tumors as malignant or benign. We implemented and evaluated multiple machine learning models, each of which was assessed based on accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. My primary contribution to this project was developing the Neural Network model, which involved designing and fine-tuning a multi-layer perceptron using Keras and TensorFlow. I implemented a three-layer neural network architecture, optimizing hyperparameters such as learning rate, batch size, and activation functions to enhance performance. To improve model generalization, I applied data normalization, dropout regularization, and hyperparameter tuning using Keras Tuner. Additionally, I conducted extensive performance evaluations using our key metrics, correlation heatmaps, confusion matrices, and ROC curves, ensuring our model’s robustness in distinguishing between malignant and benign tumors. I also contributed to the report and presentation, detailing the Neural Network model’s implementation, findings, and its potential applications in healthcare AI. This project showcased my expertise in deep learning, model optimization, and medical data analysis, as well as my ability to apply AI techniques to real-world problems in healthcare. Future improvements include expanding the dataset to enhance generalization and integrating techniques to improve model interpretability for clinical use.
